concept.technique_name: factorising a general second-degree equation into two straight lines

examples.problem_statement: When does a general-equation represent two straight lines? Say, 12x² +7xy−10y²+13x+45y−35=0

solution.result: \begin{aligned}ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 \\ a=12 \\ h=\frac{7}{2} \\ b=-10 \\ g=\frac{13}{2} \\ f=\frac{45}{2} \\ c=-35\end{aligned}
solution.description: Match the equation against the standard form, remembering that the printed xy, x and y coefficients are 2h, 2g and 2f. Halving 7, 13 and 45 gives h = 7/2, g = 13/2 and f = 45/2, alongside a = 12, b = -10 and c = -35.

solution.operation: Check condition for pair of straight lines
solution.description: State the test that decides the question: a general second-degree equation breaks into two straight lines exactly when the determinant expression abc + 2fgh - a f squared - b g squared - c h squared comes out zero. The whole problem now reduces to evaluating one number.
Substitute the six coefficients read off in step 1 into that determinant expression, keeping every halved coefficient as a fraction so nothing is rounded away before the terms cancel.

Evaluate the five terms one at a time with the sign the formula assigns each: abc gives 4200, 2fgh gives 4095/4, a f squared gives 12150/2 to be subtracted, and the last two subtractions turn positive because b and c are negative, contributing 1690/4 and 1715/4.
Add the five terms as decimals: 4200 plus 1023.75 minus 6075 plus 422.5 plus 428.75 is exactly 0. The condition is satisfied, so the equation does represent a pair of straight lines.

Having answered yes, start building the lines themselves. Factorise only the second-degree part, 12x squared + 7xy - 10y squared, into (3x - 2y)(4x + 5y); these two brackets fix the directions of the two lines.
Assume the full equation factorises into those same two brackets with unknown constants p and q added. The quadratic part already matches, so only the linear and constant parts remain to be fitted.
Expand the assumed product and set it equal to the original equation. This makes the x coefficient 4p + 3q, the y coefficient 5p - 2q and the constant pq, each of which must match 13, 45 and -35.
Read off the two equations that comparing the x and y coefficients supplies: 4p + 3q = 13 and 5p - 2q = 45. Two equations for two unknowns is exactly what is needed.
Solve that pair by substitution. Rearranging the first equation gives q = (13 - 4p)/3, and putting that expression into the second leaves a single equation in p alone.
Clear the fraction and collect terms: 23p = 161, so p = 7. Feeding p = 7 back into the rearranged first equation gives q = (13 - 28)/3 = -5.
Put p = 7 and q = -5 into the assumed brackets to get the complete factorisation (3x - 2y + 7)(4x + 5y - 5) = 0. The product pq is 7 times -5 = -35, matching the constant term as a final check.
A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero, so set each bracket to zero. That gives the two straight lines 3x - 2y + 7 = 0 and 4x + 5y - 5 = 0.

key_reminders: {'point': 'By the Vedic method, however, we at once apply the “Ādyamādyena” Sūtra and (by merely looking at the quadratic) write down the answer: Yes; and the straight lines are 3x−2y=−7 and 4x+5y=5.'}
{'point': 'This demonstrates a speed trick — immediate factorization using Vedic sutra without lengthy computation.'}
common_mistakes: Reading h, g and f straight off the equation as 7, 13 and 45 instead of halving them to 7/2, 13/2 and 45/2, which wrecks every term of the determinant.
Losing a sign: b = -10 and c = -35 are negative, so the terms built from them come out positive, not negative.
Trying to factorise the whole equation in one go rather than factorising 12x squared + 7xy - 10y squared first and fitting the constants p and q afterwards.

examples.problem_statement: Convert the vulgar fraction 1/19 into its equivalent decimal form, noting that the denominator ends in 9.

solution.description: Since the denominator ends with 9, we use the Nikhilam sutra. The base is the next power of 10 (20), and the deviation is the difference from the base.

solution.operation: Set up the division using the Vedic method
solution.description: We'll use the Vedic division method where we'll generate digits from right to left using the deviation.
The first digit is found by multiplying the previous digit (1) by the deviation (1) and adding any carry. Since this is the first step, we use 1 as the starting point.

solution.operation: Generate subsequent digits using the pattern
solution.description: The multiplier is 5 because 1/2 = 0.5, and we're working in base 20. Each digit is generated by multiplying the previous digit by 5 and taking the units digit, with appropriate carry-over.
Following the pattern: 1×5=5, 5×5=25 (write 5, carry 2), 2×5+2=12 (write 2, carry 1), 6×5+1=31 (write 1, carry 3), and so on until we return to 1.
The sequence repeats every 18 digits, as verified by the fact that 19-1=18, which is the length of the repetend.
Multiplying the result by 19 should give us 0.999... which equals 1, confirming our answer is correct.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember: The Vedic method is presented as a one-line mental method, implying speed and efficiency over the current (standard) long division method.'}
{'point': 'Caution: The modus operandi (methodology) is not fully explained on this page but will be detailed in the next few pages.'}
{'point': 'Speed tip: The Vedic methods allow conversion without lengthy division by recognizing patterns specific to denominators ending in 9.'}

concept.technique_name: Ekadhikena Purvena recurring decimal by multiplication
concept.sub_category: Ekadhikena Purvena (One More than the Previous)

examples.problem_statement: Compute decimal expansion of 1/19 using Vedic one-line mental arithmetic.

solution.operation: Start with last digit 1 (from 1/19), multiply by 2 (Ekadhikena Purvena: one more than previous, so 1+1=2)
solution.description: The last digit of 19 is 9 and the digit before it is 1, so Ekadhikena Purvena hands us the multiplier 2. Begin from the numerator 1 as the rightmost digit of the answer and multiply it by 2 to get 2.

solution.operation: Write down 2, no carry. Next digit: 2 × 2 = 4
solution.description: Record 2 as the next digit to the left; nothing is carried. Multiply that 2 by the multiplier to get 4.
Record 4 and multiply it by 2, giving 8. Still no carry to track.
Record 8 and multiply by 2, giving 16 - the first product that spills over into two digits.
Write the units digit 6 and hold the 1 as a carry. The next product is 6 times 2 plus that carried 1, which is 13.
Write 3 and carry 1. Continue with 3 times 2 plus the carry, giving 7.
Write 7; there is no carry this time. Multiplying 7 by 2 gives 14.
Write 4 and carry 1. The next product is 4 times 2 plus 1, which is 9.
Write 9 with no carry, then multiply 9 by 2 to get 18.
Write 8 and carry 1. Next comes 8 times 2 plus 1, which is 17.
Write 7 and carry 1. Next is 7 times 2 plus 1, which is 15.
Write 5 and carry 1. Next is 5 times 2 plus 1, which is 11.
Write 1 and carry 1. Next is 1 times 2 plus 1, which is 3.
Write 3 with no carry, then multiply 3 by 2 to get 6.
Write 6 with no carry, then multiply 6 by 2 to get 12.
Write 2 and carry 1. Next is 2 times 2 plus 1, which is 5.
Write 5 with no carry, then multiply 5 by 2 to get 10.

Write 0 and carry 1. The final product, 0 times 2 plus 1, returns us to the 1 we started from, so the cycle closes after 18 digits. Read the digits leftward from the start and the expansion is 0.052631578947368421 repeating.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember: This Vedic technique reduces 18-step division work into a compact, mental one-line multiplication with carries.'}
{'point': 'Caution: Do not skip carry-over steps — accuracy depends on precise tracking.'}
{'point': 'Speed tip: Practice digit-by-digit multiplication with immediate carry handling to build mental fluency.'}
{'point': 'Note: The recurring decimal is marked with dots on first and last digits to signal full repetition cycle.'}
common_mistakes: Reading the digits in the order they were produced. They are generated right to left, so the last digit found is the one that sits just after the decimal point.
Dropping a carry, for instance following 16 with 6 times 2 = 12 instead of 6 times 2 plus 1 = 13.
Stopping after a fixed count of digits instead of continuing until the running digit comes back to the starting 1, which is what marks the end of the cycle.

examples.problem_statement: Calculate the recurring decimal for 1/29 using Vedic methods.

solution.description: 29 sits just below the round number 30, so take 30 as the base and note that 29 is 1 below it. Working against 30 rather than 29 is what makes the rest of the division easy.

solution.operation: Set up the division using the sutra
solution.description: Rewrite 1/29 as 1/(30 - 1), pull the 1/30 outside, and expand what is left as an endless sum of powers of 1/30. Each successive power contributes less than the one before.
Work the first few powers out as decimals - 1/30, 1/900, 1/27000, 1/810000 - so the shrinking contributions and the places they land in become visible.

solution.operation: Build the decimal using the Vedic method
solution.description: Add those overlapping contributions place by place, which is exactly the one-line Vedic division: divide by the base's 3, carry each remainder into the next place, and the digits 0, 3, 4, 4, 8, 2, 7 and so on fall out in order.
Check the work by multiplying the expansion back by 29. Recovering 1 confirms that no digit was misplaced and no remainder was dropped along the way.
Mark the repeating block. 29 is prime and its cycle here runs the full 28 digits, so the whole string 0344827586206896551724137931 repeats without end.

solution.operation: Identify the pattern using Vedic Math sutra 'Ekadhikena Purvena' (By one more than the previous one)
solution.description: 49 is awkward on its own, but doubling top and bottom turns 1/49 into 2/98, and 98 sits just below 100. Rewriting the fraction as 2/(100 - 2) sets up a clean base of 100.
State the general expansion for a denominator of the form ten to the power n minus a. Here n = 2 and a = 2, which is precisely the 100 - 2 just obtained.

solution.operation: Substitute values and expand the series
solution.description: Substitute those values: the fraction becomes 2/100 times the series 1 + 2/100 + 4/10000 + 8/1000000 and onward, a geometric series whose common ratio is 0.02.
Write the first few terms as decimals: 0.02, then 0.0004, 0.000008, 0.00000016, 0.0000000032. Each is the previous term times 0.02, which is why the digits keep doubling two places further along.
Add the terms, letting the places where they overlap carry into one another, to build the running expansion 0.020408163265306122448. The full repeating block for 1/49 is 42 digits long.
Verify by multiplying the digits found by 49. The product is a string of nines that equals 1 to the precision kept, so the expansion is correct as far as it was taken.

Writing the doubling pattern 02, 04, 08, 16, 32 out side by side without letting 16 and 32 carry into the place ahead of them, which corrupts every digit after that point.
Treating the visible run 020408163265 as the whole cycle; the repeating block of 1/49 is 42 digits long.

examples.problem_statement: Multiply 9 by 7 using the Nikhilam Sutra method.

solution.description: Since both numbers are close to 10, we use 10 as our base for the Nikhilam method.
Calculate how much each number is less than the base (10). These are called the deviations.
Set up the numbers with their deviations written to the right. The negative signs indicate the numbers are below the base.
Add either number to the other's deviation. Both ways give the same result for the left part of the answer.
Multiply the deviations to get the right part of the answer. Negative times negative gives positive.
The left part (6) and right part (3) are combined to form the final answer.

examples.problem_statement: Multiply 6 by 7 using the Vedic method with base 10.

solution.description: Take 10 as the base and measure each factor against it: 7 falls 3 short of 10 and 6 falls 4 short, so the deficits are 3 and 4.
Cross-subtract for the left portion: 7 minus the other number's deficit of 4, or 6 minus the other number's deficit of 3. Both give 3, and matching answers confirm the step.
Multiply the two deficits vertically for the right portion. Each deficit is negative, so a negative times a negative gives +12.
Base 10 leaves room for only one digit on the right, and 12 has two. Carry the leading 1 across to the left portion, turning 3 into 3 + 1 = 4.
The left portion is now 4 and the right portion is the 2 that remains, so reading them together gives the answer 42.

{'point': 'Caution: Only one digit is permitted on the right-hand side when using base 10; any surplus must be carried over.'}
{'point': 'Speed tip: Use cross-subtraction for left portion and vertical multiplication for right portion — it’s fast once you internalize the carry rule.'}

Cross-subtracting the two deficits from each other (4 - 3) rather than subtracting one number's deficit from the other number.
